Athletic LIVE NBA Updates NFL Projections CFP Projections Fantasy Football Central Play The making of an MVP: How Pete Crow-Armstrong became the best player on the planet
 Pete Crow-Armstrong is expected to be named National League MVP on Thursday night. Illustration: Eamonn Dalton / The Athletic; Photo: Steph Chambers / Getty Images 
 By Patrick Mooney Nov. 12, 2026 5:01 am EST Updated Share article 81 LAS VEGAS — Quintin Berry was trying to defuse the situation. The Chicago Cubs third-base coach grabbed Pete Crow-Armstrong and moved him away from the umpires, like a football lineman pushing a blocking sled during two-a-day practices, steering the superstar away from a possible ejection.
 This was a getaway game in late August, starting at 12:41 p.m. local time in Phoenix, the controlled temperature set at 76 degrees inside Chase Field with the roof closed. Even during the dog days of the baseball season, Crow-Armstrong was locked in.
 Advertisement
 As soon as Crow-Armstrong’s movement off third base distracted left-hander Eduardo Rodriguez, both Crow-Armstrong and Berry gestured toward the mound, believing the pitcher had just committed a balk that would give the Cubs a 1-0 lead over the Arizona Diamondbacks, another team in the wild-card hunt.
 Berry, 41, still appears to be in the same shape that made him a pinch-running specialist for World Series contenders during his playing career. When crew chief Alfonso Márquez announced it was not a balk, Berry sprung into action and corralled Crow-Armstrong, an emotional player with uncommon power and speed.
 “I was pissed, he was pissed,” Berry recalled. “I told him: ‘Dude, we lose you, we lose the game. That’s how important you are. I don’t care what’s happening right now. Your whole focus is to stay in the game.’”
 Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago’s fiery star, captured baseball fans’ attention this summer. (Ross D. Franklin / Associated Press) That moment illustrated the spirit of the National League MVP Award that Crow-Armstrong is expected to win on Thursday night when the Baseball Writers’ Association of America announces the results from its year-end voting.
 The numbers that Crow-Armstrong posted are irrefutable: 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases to become the seventh member of Major League Baseball’s 40-40 club , plus the defensive metrics that made him a Platinum Glove center fielder .
 In essence, though, this is the MVP question: Where would the Cubs be without PCA? His ability to change every game, at any given moment, in several different ways led Berry to restrain Crow-Armstrong that afternoon inside Chase Field.
 “You have to think of it as a hard foul in basketball,” Berry explained, “when somebody’s trying to get you ejected because they want you to fight. If they do that, they win, we lose. You have to have control here.
 “I had to literally tell him that every pitch: ‘Don’t say it. I know you want to say something. Don’t say anything. I’ll talk to him for you. You cannot get kicked out of this game.’”
 What You Should Read Next 
 Even Cubs legends are in awe of Pete Crow-Armstrong’s MVP campaign
 Pete Crow-Armstrong once again stole the show this weekend at Wrigley Field.
 In terms of fWAR ( 10.6 ) and bWAR ( 9.8 ), Crow-Armstrong produced arguably the best individual season in the 150-year history of a franchise that was founded in 1876, the year Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone.
 Advertisement
 With a game built for iPhones and highlights on social media, as well as a free-flowing approach to media interviews, Crow-Armstrong captured fans’ attention and provoked reactions.
 With additional fame and new money — he agreed to a six-year, $115 million contract extension before Opening Day — Crow-Armstrong needed that team concept to feel tethered.
 “Approaching every day with winning in mind has gotten me here,” Crow-Armstrong said, “and started all these conversations about MVP and all that crap.”
 Pete Crow-Armstrong became the seventh member of MLB’s 40-40 club this season. (David Banks / Imagn Images) Ultimately, Crow-Armstrong did not get ejected for his reaction to that blown balk call, but the Cubs still lost, which put him in a mood to blast the umpires: “They find new ways to screw something up every day.”
 Taking the hoops analogy one step further, Berry referenced Kobe Bryant and Kevin Garnett, two legendary NBA competitors.
 “The great ones definitely got some things going on,” Berry said. “There’s a lot of dog in there. You don’t have to always like it. It’s not going to always look like everybody else. But that’s what separates them. That’s what makes them the 1 percentile.”
 In that rare air of Chicago’s high-profile athletes, Crow-Armstrong has developed a friendship with Bears quarterback Caleb Williams. They have attended games at the United Center together, watching the Bulls and Blackhawks from the VIP seats. Crow-Armstrong is a frequent visitor to Soldier Field, and Williams showed up at Wrigley Field to lead a round of “M-V-P” chants.
 Those who live in Chicago — a sprawling, sports-obsessed city that is a patchwork of different neighborhoods — love this kind of stuff. But it is not just for show.
 Conversations with Williams piqued Crow-Armstrong’s curiosity about how NFL players train during the season and what could be applied to the 162-game marathon.
 Advertisement
 Crow-Armstrong was not satisfied with how his breakthrough 2025 campaign ended. He reached the All-Star break with 25 home runs but tailed off in the second half, hitting only one homer in August and waiting until the final weekend of the regular season to notch his 30th and 31st.
 Looking for answers, Crow-Armstrong bounced some ideas off Mark Weisman, a major-league strength and conditioning coach he had previously worked with in Chicago’s farm system.
 Weisman also offered a different kind of credibility as someone who had been a high-level athlete, a bruising running back for the Iowa Hawkeyes, good enough to get a tryout with the Cincinnati Bengals.
 “Caleb told Pete about what you do in football,” Weisman said. “Granted, you don’t play every day. In football, you play once a week, so they can train a different way. Early in the week, you can push the lower-body movements a lot more. As you go along in the week, you’ll have a more dynamic-type training.
 “It’s also physically demanding. You have to move other human beings and be able to absorb hits, right? Versus in baseball, you’re inflicting it with an object. It’s rotational. The goal is to get Pete as strong as he can, but you don’t want to put on much weight, if any. (We) don’t want to lose the other attributes that make him great.”
 Bears quarterback Caleb Williams became friends with Pete Crow-Armstrong, which led to conversations about training for the Cubs star. (Matt Marton / Imagn Images) The Cubs did not design football-style workouts for Crow-Armstrong. Rather, the idea was to create a stronger foundation heading into the 2026 season, and then devise a plan for a once-per-series workout dedicated to certain concepts, focusing on high-intensity movements at a lower volume so that he would feel game-ready.
 As Crow-Armstrong widened the gap with Shohei Ohtani in the NL MVP race, the Cubs continued to track his workload and performance, measuring a 24-year-old player who’s listed at 6-foot, 184 pounds . In September, Weisman noted that Crow-Armstrong’s bat speed, exit velocities and sprint speeds were all holding strong.
 Advertisement
 That Crow-Armstrong would take the initiative to help redesign his offseason program was telling. He also listened to feedback from teammates and Cubs manager Craig Counsell, suggestions on how to better control his emotions and pressure situations.
 What You Should Read Next 
 Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong joins MLB’s 40-40 club, putting exclamation point on MVP campaign
 Crow-Armstrong has been putting the finishing touches on arguably the best individual season in the club’s long history.
 As a hitter, Crow-Armstrong goes more by feel than analysis of his mechanics. But his adjustments were dramatic enough that major-league evaluators struggled to recall other players who successfully changed their approach to such a degree.
 In the batter’s box, Crow-Armstrong exhibited a new level of discipline without sacrificing his aggressiveness. After drawing 53 walks over his first 293 major-league games spread over three seasons , he walked 83 times this year. He also did damage against left-handed pitching ( .879 OPS ), closing another weakness.
 Winning an MVP sets an almost impossibly high standard for the rest of a player’s career. At this point, Crow-Armstrong understands those adjustments will never stop.
 “You commit to something and it works and you wonder why you can’t do that every at-bat,” Crow-Armstrong said. “That’s just the nature of the game. That’s what’s hard about baseball.”
 Standing on the grass in his position as Chicago’s first-base coach, Jose Javier could feel the energy and anticipation at Wrigley Field as Crow-Armstrong neared a historic achievement. The images on the video board and the noise from the crowd heightened the 40-40 countdown.
 In his role, Javier would also often be on the edges of the camera shots whenever Crow-Armstrong slammed his helmet to the ground or paused to rein in those impulses.
 “He’s mad at himself,” Javier said. “He’s not mad at anybody else. He’s just mad that he didn’t get the hit, or he didn’t hit the ball hard. I’m OK with that because I know he’s just mad at the situation.
 Advertisement
 “It looks bad on TV, but he cares so much about the team. He cares so much about his teammates. He just wants to win.”
 Pete Crow-Armstrong finished the 2026 season with 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases. (Michael Reaves / Getty Images) Underlining that point, Crow-Armstrong launched his 40th home run on Sept. 6 in Miami, but he did not steal his 40th base until Sept. 24 at the Friendly Confines .
 Instead of chasing numbers or padding his stats, Crow-Armstrong stayed attuned to game situations, taking into account Wrigley Field’s hitter-friendly environment this year. The calculated risks also changed with the addition of Alex Bregman to an explosive lineup, lessening the need to manufacture runs with a station-to-station offense.
 “We probably left a lot of stolen bases on the table,” Javier said, “but when the team needs it, he’s going to have the bag.”
 Crow-Armstrong did not steal all those bases with pure speed alone. He also mastered the subtle fundamentals, creating momentum with his stances and pre-pitch movements.
 In this part of the 40-40 equation, Javier compared it to two cars idling in front of a red light. If one is completely stopped, and the other is slightly behind but moving slowly before the light turns green, it’s obvious which car will accelerate faster.
 Pete Crow-Armstrong’s momentum steal lead is a masterclass in baserunning mechanics. 
Watch how an early probing shuffle baits the Padres into a mid-shuffle drop-glove pick—and how PCA uses the 12-foot safety zone to redirect and beat it.👇 pic.twitter.com/j6AqXVqQW2 
 — Kevin Graber M.Ed. (@Coach_KGraber) September 8, 2026 
 “He gets frustrated,” Javier said. “But how quickly he can just let it go and focus on the next at-bat, the next play, it’s incredible. He makes the switch.”
 Crow-Armstrong did not have enough time to turn it on for the playoffs , going 0-for-7 with four strikeouts and a walk as the San Diego Padres swept the Cubs out of the wild-card round after two games at Petco Park . For club officials, that felt like a wasted opportunity, squandering what could go down as a once-in-a-lifetime season.
 Advertisement
 Inside ARIA, the hotel and casino on the Las Vegas Strip hosting MLB’s annual meetings for general managers, the Cubs have focused on pitching this week , trying to build a better supporting cast and gather information before the owners’ anticipated lockout.
 Crow-Armstrong has always been generous with dishing out credit, name-dropping teammates and coaches who shared knowledge, showed patience and helped him develop. But every MVP has to be the CEO of his own career, and PCA now knows that his way works.
 “It sounds corny, but conviction comes from within,” Crow-Armstrong said. “It’s up to me to do that, and to feel that way. When I’ve had success this year, that’s been me feeling convicted. And that comes from me.”
